textRun.content: Objective: robot at deployment executing a task
in an unseen situation at training
Learn how to grasp and move
across variations of the same task.
so the policy can use suitable actions.
Working hypothesis: generalizable behavior and useful environmental context support adaptation.

We investigate how a robot can handle a deployment situation it did not encounter during training. The idea has two components. First, the controller needs a repertoire of grasping and movement behavior that generalizes within a task. Second, the system needs a useful interpretation of its current environment so that the conditioned policy can produce appropriate commands. These are research hypotheses, not guarantees provided by reinforcement learning. The task remains pick and lift with a consistent top-down grasp strategy. This framing follows the latest proposal: policy generalization is now an explicit enabling part of the study, while initial environment estimation remains a separate component.
We propose a policy trained with classical inputs and high impact environmental parameters can learn variation of movment.
Assumption to test: varied training produces a policy capable of executing at held-out heights.

We assume an RL framework. The policy receives standard robot and task state plus a compact set of environmental parameters, and learns grasping and movement commands from task reward. During simulation training, selected environmental values can be supplied from the simulator. During estimated-context evaluation, the corresponding values must come from the estimator. RL is a method of training the controller; successful generalization must still be measured. Selected context variables could be guided by the existing CREST workflow, but no completed CREST selection is claimed here. The current policy has 45 state values including object pose, relative geometry, supplied weight, and finger-force observations. If the future estimator predicts height or pose, true copies and derived versions of those quantities must not bypass that estimator.
We train a visual estimator based off objects with different materials, size and a measured weight. With a single type of material.
Scope: one material, fixed density and friction, fixed camera. This tests interpolation over size.

Completed evidence: the saved initial-image CNN achieved test mean absolute mass error of 2.760891 g and RMSE 4.434443 g on 12 held-out cube sizes and 48 images. The constant training-mean predictor had 106.373742 g test MAE. The complete dataset contains 96 sizes and 384 images; all views of one object stay in one split. The model checkpoint was selected by validation loss, not test results. This is a controlled visual size-to-mass prior: density, material, friction, camera and background are fixed. It does not establish general mass inference for identical-looking objects of different densities. It is not a height-estimation result. Data source: runs/visual_mass/initial_rgb_mass/model/metrics.json. Plot: runs/visual_mass/initial_rgb_mass/model/predictions.png.
The full pipeline runs in simulation(fornow)
Initial RGB image(one time) → mass estimate → supplied policy input → pick-and-lift execution.
Current run: model weights and the mass estimate remain fixed.

Completed integration demonstration: three configured cases, one seed per cube size, each completed the full 50-action, 2.5-second rollout and ended with task success and a grasp. The 4, 5 and 6 cm cubes had masses 64, 125 and 216 g; predicted masses were approximately 62.32, 121.24 and 212.45 g. Across the three trials the mass MAE was 2.996986 g. The estimate remained fixed throughout each episode. Final continuous success lasted about 2.10, 2.10 and 2.05 simulated seconds. These images are actual saved simulation frames. This establishes that the components can run together. Three trials are not a reliability estimate, and there is no matched true-estimate-versus-fixed-estimate benefit comparison here. The run used a saved frozen-movement/independent-strength v1 checkpoint, not a newly trained policy that generalizes over initial object elevation. Source: runs/deployment/20261022_014201_067220/summary.json and manifest.json.
